https://www.thetimes.com/uk/science/arti.title: Bleak future for Italian farmers as climate change dries up Po River
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/science/arti.text:
The rich, fertile land along the Po River has for centuries been Italy’s breadbasket. Generations of farmers have thrived along the mighty waterway’s 405-mile course, from its descent from the Alps to the nutrient-rich delta where it spills out into the Adriatic.
This year, however, has been different. Farmers who planted their winter crops on the delta plain, within 100m of the meandering waterway, have seen mass failures. Fields that should be lush with wheat are blackened and dead.
The Po was much lower than usual because of the latest in a series of freak winter droughts but that alone did not explain the wilting crops.
“What happened is the river slowed to such an extent that seawater flowed 15km back upstream from the Adriatic, and salt is now seeping into the earth, killing off our crops,” Giancarlo Mantovani, the head of a consortium that maintains the river banks, said.
As the Po turns from a precious source of water at its delta to a salty pollutant, fears are growing that climate change is slowly crippling the viability of the land. The Po valley has just suffered its second hottest winter in 40 years, rainfall has fallen to 60 per cent below average, and the run-off from melting snow in the Alps is also expected to be down by 70 per cent.
“It’s the third driest winter in the last 60 years, the temperature has been rising to 18C during the day and when you add in the lack of snow in the Alps, things are explosive here,” Andrea Gavazzoli, an official with the ADBPO, a state agency monitoring the river’s health, said.
Where it passes close to Ferrara, near the delta, the Po’s flow is down to 700 cubic metres a second from the average of 1,500 for this time of year, Mantovani said.
“The record drop was in 2006, when it fell to 189 cubic metres, the salt ebbed 30km inland and salt water came out of people’s taps,” he said.
“But that was in July, in the middle of summer, when the Po was depleted as farmers along it took water to irrigate their fields.
Right now, no one is watering but they are due to start in 15 days, and I predict we will fall to 200 cubic metres and the salty sea water will push further inland.”
It is a humiliating fate for the river that has given Italy its largest fertile plain, measures 500m across at its widest point and threads through cities including Turin, Piacenza and Cremona before pumping out so much silt its delta extends by 200 acres a year.
The valley experienced droughts in 2007, 2012 and 2017, and it is the growing frequency that points to climate change, Carlo Cacciamani, the head of Italy’s national meteorological and climatology agency, said.
“This starts with rising temperatures, which means summer heat of 39C is now becoming almost normal in the Po valley,” he said. “High pressure then reduces rainfall, albeit with extreme events where the rain is so heavy the land cannot absorb it,” he added.
The results this winter have been startling. In Boscone Cusani, on the banks of the Po in the region of Emilia-Romagna, residents discovered the remains of a 19th-century boat as the water level lowered. In Viadana, where the Po separates Emilia-Romagna from the region of Lombardy, people from both sides met on a new island that has formed in the middle of the river.
Right across Italy, climate change is playing havoc with weather and often it means more rather than less water, with a suspected hurricane claiming victims as it flooded Catania in Sicily last year.
Avocados, mangos and passion fruit are now being grown on the slopes of nearby Mount Etna as olive tree planters slowly work their way further north in Italy, taking advantage of warmer weather.
The environmental group Legambiente recently said that even if governments managed to keep the global temperature rise down to 1.5C, a third of Italy’s Alpine glaciers would be gone by the end of the century.
If the 1.5C target is not met, they will all vanish. Monte Viso, the mountain near the French border where the Po originates, is slowly crumbling as the permafrost holding it together melts, with 200,000 cubic metres of rock tumbling from it in 2020.
The author Tobias Jones said the suffering of the Po had extra significance given the river’s importance to Italy.
“Iconic battles were fought there and it was a moat defending Italy from invaders from the time of Hannibal to the Holy Roman Empire, while today 40 per cent of Italian GDP is produced in its watershed,” said Jones, who has travelled the length of the river and will publish a book, The Po, about it this year.
Jones said he tried to locate the river near the town of Saluzzo in the Piedmont region last summer but only found dry gravel.
“You cannot simply mislay the largest river in Italy, so I asked a farmer and he said ‘It often disappears’. I noticed he was working a pump to draw water from the aquifer, and I realised that was part of the problem.”
Stefano Ciafani, the head of Legambiente, said it was crucial that farmers figured out ways to reduce the water they drain from the Po. “Water jets used in fields lose half the water in the air as droplets evaporate. We should switch to pipes laid along the earth from which water flows,” he said.
Experts are also pushing for the creation of more small lakes to collect and preserve rainwater for use in agriculture during droughts.
The town of Reggio Emilia now recycles five million cubic metres of water from sewage a year to irrigate farmland, meaning farmers do not need to drain the Po.
“A lot more needs to be done because otherwise Italian agriculture and the Mediterranean diet that is renowned around the world will succumb to desertification and tropicalisation,” Ciafani said. “This water is not coming back, not at least until climate change is acted on.”
